```{r}
#| include: false
library(here); library(tidyverse); library(knitr)
fit    <- read_csv(here("results/tables/preston_fit.csv"))
gaps   <- read_csv(here("results/tables/income_group_gaps.csv"))
latest <- as.integer(readLines(here("results/tables/latest_year.txt")))
dbl_0  <- fit$per_doubling[fit$year == 1990]
dbl_1  <- fit$per_doubling[fit$year == latest]
gap_0  <- gaps$gap_high_low[gaps$year == 1990]
gap_1  <- gaps$gap_high_low[gaps$year == latest]
```

## Question and motivation

Richer countries tend to have healthier populations, but is the relationship strong,
does it flatten out at high incomes, and have poor countries been catching up? This matters
because if life expectancy depends on income alone, growth is the main lever; if the curve itself
shifts over time (through medicine, sanitation, vaccines), health can improve even without growth.
This relationship is known as the **Preston curve**. I use it to ask: *how has the link between
income and life expectancy changed between 1990 and `r latest`?*

## Data

All data come from the World Bank's World Development Indicators, downloaded directly in R with
the `WDI` package (see `code/01_get_data.R`):

- **GDP per capita, PPP, constant 2021 international dollars.** Per-capita removes the effect of country size; PPP adjusts for price-level differences; *constant* dollars remove inflation so 1990 and `r latest` are comparable.
- **Life expectancy at birth** (years).
- **Population**, used for bubble sizes and population-weighted averages.

I drop World Bank aggregates (World, regions, income groups) and keep country-year observations with all three variables. Because GDP is plotted on a log scale (a $1,000 gain matters far more to a country at $2,000 than at $60,000), I model life expectancy as a function of log income.

## Figure 1: The cross-section today

```{r}
#| echo: false
include_graphics(here("results/figures/fig1_preston_latest.png"))
```

The curve is steep at low incomes and flat at high incomes. Estimated from a regression of life
expectancy on log GDP per capita, a **doubling of income is associated with about
`r round(dbl_1, 1)` additional years** of life expectancy in `r latest`. There is also wide
dispersion around the line: countries at similar incomes differ by many years, so income is not destiny.
This is a correlation, not a causal effect; health also raises income.

## Figure 2: The curve shifts

```{r}
#| echo: false
include_graphics(here("results/figures/fig2_curve_shift.png"))
```

The 1990 and `r latest` curves are plotted together. The `r latest` curve sits above the 1990 curve:
countries at the same income live longer today than in 1990, which points to
non-income factors (medical technology, public health, vaccines). The arrows show that individual countries
both moved right (growth) and up (health gains). The slope per income doubling was
`r round(dbl_0, 1)` years in 1990 and `r round(dbl_1, 1)` years in `r latest`.

## Figure 3: Convergence across income groups

```{r}
#| echo: false
include_graphics(here("results/figures/fig3_income_groups.png"))
```

Population-weighted life expectancy rose in every income group. The gap between high- and
low-income countries was **`r round(gap_0, 1)` years in 1990** and is
**`r round(gap_1, 1)` years in `r latest`**. The figure also shows the temporary setback around 2020 to 2021,
which coincides with COVID-19. (Note: income groups use the World Bank's *current* classification, so a country
that grew rich is counted as high-income for all years.)

## Takeaway

Income and life expectancy are strongly and non-linearly related: gains per extra dollar are largest
for the poorest countries. But income is not the whole story. The curve itself has moved upward
since 1990, and the life expectancy gap between rich and poor countries has changed substantially,
so health progress has partly been "free" of income growth. For policy, this suggests investments in
low-cost health technology can pay off even where growth is slow.

**Limitations.** The analysis is descriptive; income groups are fixed at today's classification;
and national averages hide inequality within countries.
